covers.quote: Keep sentences short to help people scan content.
Sometimes it’s hard to avoid longer sentences – for example, if you have to include a long department name.

rules.quote: Keep sentences to an average of 15 words and no more than 25 words, especially for digital content.
rules.specification: Treat 15 words as an upper average-length target, not a requirement that shorter sentences be lengthened. The page acknowledges unavoidable longer sentences but does not specify an averaging method or a word-counting convention.
rules.violation_condition: A document's sentences exceed the average-length target of 15 words, or an individual sentence exceeds 25 words without an unavoidable reason.
when: Applies especially to digital content, but is not limited to it.
Longer sentences may be unavoidable, for example when a long department name must be included.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the sentence-length targets, their introductory summary and the acknowledged exception.

rules.quote: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.
rules.specification: What counts as unusual depends on the intended audience. The page does not define an audience vocabulary or a required location for explanations.
rules.violation_condition: An unusual word, phrase or idiom appears without an explanation that makes it understandable to the intended audience.
when: An unusual expression is acceptable when it is explained.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: avoiding and explaining are alternative ways to satisfy one check, not separate rules.

rules.quote: Expand all acronyms on their first use.
rules.violation_condition: The first occurrence of an acronym has no expansion.
when: Check the first use of each acronym.
rules.why: The first-use expansion check is distinct from the neighbouring check for unexplained unusual expressions.

rules.quote: Level AAA requires a lower secondary education reading level, after removal of proper names and titles (year 7 or between 12 and 14 years old).
rules.specification: The page identifies the required education level but supplies no assessment method or readability formula. Do not substitute a particular formula without review.
rules.violation_condition: Web content intended to meet the cited Level AAA criterion requires a reading level above lower secondary education after proper names and titles are excluded.
when: Applies when assessing conformance with the cited WCAG Level AAA reading-level criterion.
Exclude proper names and titles from the reading-level assessment.
rules.why: G-2: retain the explicit requirement together with its conformance condition and exclusions.

covers.quote: Use active rather than passive voice.

examples.note: The contrasting passive sentence is explanatory, not labelled incorrect.

parts.quote: Eligible students can access the subsidy by completing the application.

examples.note: The contrasting passive sentence is explanatory, not labelled incorrect.

rules.violation_condition: A sentence uses passive voice where active voice is the preferred alternative.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates heading and body; E-1 avoids treating the explanatory passive-voice contrasts as explicitly incorrect examples.

covers.quote: Use ‘other than’ carefully
When you use ‘other than’, make sure it’s clear which words are included in the exception.

parts.quote: The graduate with a broken leg sat at the desk.
The graduate sat at the desk with a broken leg.
A person who is younger than 60, other than a teacher ...
A person other than a teacher who is younger than 60 ...

rules.quote: Write exactly what you mean and construct your sentences so there is no ambiguity.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence permits competing interpretations, including an unclear attachment or unclear scope for an exception introduced by ‘other than’.
when: When ‘other than’ introduces an exception, the words included in the exception must be clear.
rules.why: G-2: unclear exception scope is a specific case of the same ambiguity check, not a second finding.

parts.quote: Include these documents when you apply.
You can’t submit your application if you don’t include these documents.

rules.quote: Write sentences so they are positive rather than negative.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence frames its message negatively when the same message can be expressed positively.
rules.why: G-1 and E-2: the body states the positive-framing check and has its own contrast pair; the parent heading also groups other checks.

covers.quote: Avoid using double negatives.
Double negatives can lead to misunderstandings, so avoid them.

parts.quote: It was acceptable …
It was not unacceptable …

rules.violation_condition: A sentence expresses a proposition through double negation, such as ‘not unacceptable’.
when: The negatives must interact in the same proposition; merely finding two negative words in different clauses is insufficient.
rules.why: G-4: the accessibility item and explanatory body repeat the same double-negation rule.

covers.quote: Make each word work for its place in the sentence.
Keep the words that play a critical function in the sentence.
Be precise
Avoid unnecessary words. Keep the words needed to make meaning clear.
Avoid using ‘there is’ and ‘there are’ when they only add extra words and not meaning.

parts.quote: We provide statistics for trade reports. Contact us with trade data requests and we’ll respond within 2 business days.

Our team will happily provide you with any statistics you might be seeking for the purpose of producing better and more factually accurate trade reports. Let us know if you’re seeking specific trade data and we’ll seek to provide it to you as soon as we can, usually within 2 business days.
Call us if you have any questions.
If you were unsure about any of the information or needed more details, you are welcome to telephone our office to acquire what you needed.
If anything doesn’t fit within this framework ...
If there is anything that doesn’t fit within this framework ...

rules.specification: Assess whether a shorter grammatical formulation preserves the essential meaning. Do not automatically flag adjectives, adverbs or every occurrence of ‘there is’ and ‘there are’.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence contains dispensable wording that adds no necessary meaning, including semantically empty ‘there is’ or ‘there are’ constructions.
when: Retain words needed to make the meaning clear.
Flag ‘there is’ and ‘there are’ only when they add words without adding meaning.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: ‘Be precise’ repeats the unnecessary-word check, and empty existential constructions are a named case of it.

covers.quote: Vary your sentence structure to suit the content.

rules.specification: The page gives no required mix of structures or repetition threshold. Suitability must be judged against the content; do not require variation for its own sake.
rules.violation_condition: A passage uses unnecessarily uniform sentence structures when variation would better suit its content.
when: Variation must suit the content.
rules.why: G-4: consolidate heading and body; structural variety is distinct from whether an individual sentence is easy to scan.

parts.quote: You can delete your application within an hour of applying.
You can, within an hour of applying, delete your application.

rules.quote: Sentences should still be easy to scan, even using these structures.
rules.specification: The example identifies an inserted modifier that interrupts the main clause. The page supplies no general measurable boundary for scan difficulty; compound or complex structure alone is not a violation.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence's clause or modifier arrangement makes it unnecessarily difficult to scan, such as an avoidable interruption of the main clause.
when: Applies to simple, compound and complex sentences.
Compound and complex sentences may be used for variety and flow.
rules.why: E-2: the scanability instruction, not the broader variety heading, is the nearest rule tested by the modifier-placement contrast.

covers.quote: For example, use a verb instead of the noun that relates to the verb.

parts.quote: Please apply.

rules.quote: Instead of bureaucratic language, use plain language words and terms.
rules.specification: Treat the verb-versus-related-noun instruction as a case of replacing bureaucratic constructions. It targets indirect expressions for actions, not every noun derived from a verb.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence uses unnecessarily bureaucratic wording where a plain equivalent preserves the meaning, including an indirect action-noun construction replaceable by a direct verb.
when: Prefer a direct verb when a related action noun creates an unnecessarily indirect construction.
rules.why: G-2: the page explicitly introduces the verb-versus-noun construction as an example of replacing bureaucratic language.

covers.quote: Phrases that combine more than 3 adjectives or nouns are difficult to understand.
Rephrase sentences to break up strings of adjectives or noun trains.

rules.quote: Use fewer than 3 adjectives or nouns at a time
rules.specification: Confirm the boundary before enforcing strings of exactly 3: the heading says fewer than 3, while the body says more than 3 are difficult. The violating example contains a four-word noun train.
rules.violation_condition: A phrase contains a string of 3 or more adjectives or nouns under the heading's stated limit; the body discusses difficulty only for strings of more than 3.
when: Applies to strings of adjectives and noun trains, not the total number of adjectives or nouns distributed throughout a sentence.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the train-length check; E-4 requires exposing rather than silently resolving the conflicting cutoff.

parts.quote: The goal is to analyse how we can reallocate human resources. The analysis will inform our business plan.
The human resource reallocation analysis will inform our business plan.

tags.specification: Confirm the boundary before enforcing strings of exactly 3: the heading says fewer than 3, while the body says more than 3 are difficult. The violating example contains a four-word noun train.
tags.violation_condition: A phrase contains a string of 3 or more adjectives or nouns under the heading's stated limit; the body discusses difficulty only for strings of more than 3.

when: Applies to strings of adjectives and noun trains, not the total number of adjectives or nouns distributed throughout a sentence.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the train-length check; E-4 requires exposing rather than silently resolving the conflicting cutoff.

anchor.quote: Avoid using ‘if’ and ‘unless’ together

covers.quote: Don’t use words such as ‘if’ and ‘unless’ in the same sentence.

parts.quote: From 1 October, your partner can sign forms on your behalf.
If your partner signed the form on your behalf, we can accept it unless they signed it before 1 October.

tags.violation_condition: A sentence uses both ‘if’ and ‘unless’ to express its conditions.

when: The two conditional words occur in the same sentence.
rules.why: G-4: the body supplies the same-sentence scope for the heading's single conditional-word check.

anchor.quote: Don’t use the ‘such ... as’ form.

parts.quote: Take appropriate steps.
Take such steps as are appropriate.

tags.specification: Interpret the form using the example ‘such steps as are appropriate’. This is not a blanket prohibition on adjacent ‘such as’ introducing examples.
tags.violation_condition: A sentence uses the discontinuous ‘such ... as’ construction, such as a noun introduced by ‘such’ and qualified by an ‘as’ clause.

when: Applies to the discontinuous construction illustrated by the manual.
rules.why: G-1: the parent heading groups this construction and the unrelated ‘being’ construction, which need separate checks.

anchor.quote: Use ‘and’ instead of ‘being’ or ‘not being’.

parts.quote: A person who is 70 or over and has a driving licence ...
A person who is 70 or over, being a person who has a driving licence ...

tags.specification: Apply this to the qualifying construction illustrated by ‘being a person who has’. Do not flag every occurrence of ‘being’, including unrelated verb uses or nouns such as ‘human being’.
tags.violation_condition: An additional descriptive condition is attached with ‘being’ or ‘not being’ where it could instead be coordinated with ‘and’.

when: The ‘being’ or ‘not being’ construction introduces a condition that can be expressed with ‘and’.
rules.why: G-1 and E-2: this body instruction and its own contrast pair define a separate check from ‘such ... as’.
